topics.ch: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
topics.h: Why does the dosa batter rise overnight in summer but stay flat in a cold Delhi winter? Asking 'why' and then testing the answer is exactly how science works.
p: Science starts with careful observation and a question that can be tested.
A hypothesis is a possible, testable explanation, for example 'warm batter ferments faster than cold batter'.
A fair test changes only one thing (the independent variable), measures one result (the dependent variable) and keeps everything else the same (controlled variables).
Repeating an experiment and comparing results makes the conclusion more reliable.
If the evidence does not support the hypothesis, scientists change the hypothesis and test again. Results are shared so others can check them.

ex.q: Think it through: Meera wants to know if salt dissolves faster in hot water than in cold water. How should she plan a fair test?
st: Change only one thing: the temperature of the water (hot and cold).
Measure one result: the time taken for the salt to dissolve completely.
Keep the same amount of water, the same amount of salt, the same kind of glass and the same stirring.
Repeat each trial a few times and compare the average times. Use warm tap water, not boiling water, and ask an adult to help.
ex.a: Vary only the water temperature, time the dissolving, keep all else the same and repeat the trials.

topics.rl: Doctors testing a new medicine, farmers comparing two fertilisers on equal plots and ISRO engineers testing rocket parts all use fair tests.

topics.ch: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
topics.h: Nobody has seen an atom with their eyes, yet scientists can predict how atoms behave. How? They build models!
p: A scientific model is a simplified picture of something real: a physical model (a globe), a diagram (a drawing of a cell), a mathematical model (an equation) or a computer model.
Models help us explain what we see and predict what will happen next.
A good model makes predictions that can be tested by observation or experiment.
Every model has limits. A globe shows the shape of the continents but not the height of every hill.
When new evidence disagrees with a model, the model is improved or replaced, as happened with the models of the atom.

ex.q: Think it through: A model says the Moon shines only because it reflects sunlight. What does this model predict will happen when the Earth comes exactly between the Sun and the Moon?
st: If moonlight is reflected sunlight, the Moon needs sunlight to reach it.
When the Earth is exactly in between, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
So less sunlight reaches the Moon and it should look dim.
This is what we see in a lunar eclipse, so the observation supports the model.
ex.a: The Moon should become dim, which is what happens during a lunar eclipse.

topics.rl: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses computer models of the atmosphere to forecast the monsoon and warn people about cyclones.

topics.ch: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
topics.h: How many grains of rice are in a 1 kg packet? You don't need to count them all. A clever estimate gets you close in a minute!
p: Estimation means finding a sensible approximate value using things you know, simple rounding and reasoning.
A good estimate is quick and close enough to judge whether an answer is reasonable.
Scientific notation writes numbers as a × 10ⁿ, where a is at least 1 and less than 10. For example 3,50,000 = 3.5 × 10⁵.
Scientists all over the world use SI units. There are 7 SI base units, including the metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time) and kelvin (temperature).
Always check: is my answer about the right size? A classroom door 20 m tall cannot be right!

ex.q: Think it through: About how many grains of rice are in a 1 kg packet, if 100 grains weigh about 2 g?
st: 100 grains weigh about 2 g, so 1 g has about 50 grains.
Number of grains ≈ 1000 × 50 = 50 000.
In scientific notation that is about 5 × 10⁴ grains.
ex.a: About 50 000 grains (5 × 10⁴).

topics.rl: Shopkeepers estimate stock, cooks estimate rice for a wedding feast and election officials estimate how many voters a booth can handle in a day.

topics.ch: Cell: The Building Block of Life
topics.t: Discovery of cells and the cell theory
topics.h: A thin slice of cork looked like a honeycomb of tiny empty rooms under a microscope. That simple look in 1665 began the whole science of cells!
p: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his microscope, saw small box-like compartments and named them 'cells'.
In 1674 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using better lenses, was the first to see free-living cells in pond water.
In 1831 Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in plant cells.
Schleiden (1838, plants) and Schwann (1839, animals) proposed the cell theory: all plants and animals are made of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life.
In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

ex.q: Think it through: Hooke's cork cells looked empty, like little rooms with walls. Why?
st: Cork comes from the bark of a tree.
Cork cells are dead cells.
When a cell dies, its living contents are lost but its cell wall remains.
So Hooke saw only the walls of the cells.
ex.a: Cork cells are dead, so only their cell walls were left to see.

topics.rl: Every pathology lab that checks a blood sample or a biopsy under a microscope builds on the cell theory.

topics.ch: Cell: The Building Block of Life
topics.h: A cell is like a busy little city: it has a control room, power stations, factories, a packing office and even a recycling unit!
p: The cell membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances in and out and stops others. Plant cells also have a tough outer cell wall made mainly of cellulose.
The nucleus has a double membrane and contains chromosomes made of DNA. It controls the cell's activities and carries information passed on to new cells.
Mitochondria release energy from food in the form of ATP, so they are called the powerhouses of the cell. Ribosomes make proteins.

Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of channels: rough ER has ribosomes and helps make proteins; smooth ER helps make fats (lipids). The Golgi apparatus packages materials and sends them to where they are needed.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and are called 'suicide bags'. Plastids (such as chloroplasts with green chlorophyll) and a large central vacuole are found in plant cells.

ex.q: Think it through: Dry kishmish (raisins) are soaked in water overnight. In the morning they are plump. What happened?
st: The inside of a raisin has a lot of sugar and very little water.
The cell membranes of the raisin are selectively permeable.
Water moves through them from where there is more water (outside) to where there is less water (inside).
This movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is osmosis, so the raisins swell.
ex.a: Water entered the raisin cells by osmosis, so the raisins swelled.

topics.rl: Salt on cucumber slices pulls water out of the cells by osmosis, which is why salted kheera becomes watery and limp.

topics.ch: Cell: The Building Block of Life
topics.h: An Amoeba is just one cell, yet it eats, moves, breathes and divides. You are trillions of cells working as a team. Both are alive!
p: Unicellular organisms are made of a single cell that carries out all life processes. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, yeast and bacteria.
Multicellular organisms are made of many cells. Examples: Hydra, mango trees, mushrooms, earthworms and humans.
In multicellular organisms cells are specialised for different jobs, called division of labour. Nerve cells carry messages and red blood cells carry oxygen.
Cells differ in shape and size according to their job. Amoeba changes shape using pseudopodia, while nerve cells are long and branched.
Prokaryotic cells (such as bacteria) have no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi, Amoeba) have a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane.

ex.q: Think it through: Why can a single-celled Paramecium survive on its own, while a single cell taken from your liver cannot live alone in a pond?
st: A Paramecium's single cell does everything: taking in food, getting energy, removing waste and reproducing.
A liver cell is specialised for a few jobs only.
It depends on other cells, such as blood cells that bring it food and oxygen.
On its own it cannot carry out every life process.
ex.a: Paramecium's one cell performs all life processes, but a specialised liver cell depends on other cells.

topics.rl: The yeast that makes idli and dosa batter rise and the bacteria that set milk into curd are unicellular helpers in every Indian kitchen.

topics.h: Why can a bamboo shoot grow taller every day, and why is a coconut husk so tough that you need a sickle to open it? Different plant tissues are the answer!
p: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do a particular job.

Meristematic tissue has actively dividing cells with dense cytoplasm and thin walls. Apical meristem at root and shoot tips increases length; lateral meristem (cambium) increases girth; intercalary meristem at the base of leaves or internodes (as in grasses) adds length there.

Simple permanent tissues: parenchyma (thin-walled, stores food; chlorenchyma has chlorophyll; aerenchyma has big air spaces that help water plants float), collenchyma (walls thickened at the corners, gives flexibility to leaf stalks) and sclerenchyma (dead cells with thick lignin walls, gives hardness, as in coconut husk).

Complex permanent tissues are made of more than one type of cell: xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres) carries water and minerals; phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres) carries food.
Protective tissues: the epidermis covers the plant, often with a waxy cuticle, and older stems are covered by cork, whose dead cells contain suberin.

ex.q: Think it through: A lotus plant floats easily on a pond. Which tissue helps, and how?
st: The stems and leaf stalks of water plants have parenchyma with large air cavities.
This special parenchyma is called aerenchyma.
The trapped air makes the parts light.
So the plant gets buoyancy and floats.
ex.a: Aerenchyma, a parenchyma with large air spaces, gives buoyancy.

topics.rl: Coir mats and ropes made in Kerala come from the tough sclerenchyma fibres of coconut husk, and jute bags are made from plant fibres too.

topics.h: When you kick a football, three of the four main kinds of animal tissue work together in your leg in a split second: muscle, nerve and connective tissue such as bone and blood!
p: Epithelial tissue covers and lines the body. Squamous epithelium lines the mouth and blood vessels; skin has many layers (stratified squamous); cuboidal epithelium lines kidney tubules; columnar epithelium lines the intestine; ciliated columnar epithelium lines the windpipe.

Connective tissue joins and supports. Blood has a fluid matrix (plasma); bone is hard with calcium and phosphorus compounds; cartilage supports the nose and ear; tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone; areolar tissue fills spaces; adipose tissue stores fat.

Muscular tissue contracts to cause movement. Striated (skeletal) muscle is voluntary; smooth (unstriated) muscle is involuntary, as in the intestine and iris; cardiac muscle of the heart is involuntary and contracts rhythmically all through life.
Nervous tissue is made of neurons. A neuron has a cell body with a nucleus, short branched dendrites and a long axon. Neurons carry messages called nerve impulses.

ex.q: Think it through: Sana twists her ankle while playing kho-kho and the doctor says a ligament is stretched. What does a ligament do?
st: Bones at a joint must be held together but still be able to move.
Ligaments are connective tissue that join one bone to another.
They are strong and elastic.
A sudden twist can over-stretch them, causing pain and swelling.
ex.a: A ligament joins bone to bone at a joint; Sana's ankle ligament was over-stretched.

topics.rl: Physiotherapists who help cricketers recover from injuries need to know exactly which muscles, tendons and ligaments are affected.

topics.t: Tissues at work: structure and function
topics.h: On a hot afternoon a peepal tree can lose many buckets of water through its leaves, and still keep lifting more from the soil. How do its tissues manage this?
p: Every tissue is built to suit its job: thick lignin walls for strength, air spaces for floating, long axons for carrying messages over long distances.
Xylem carries water and minerals only upwards from roots; phloem carries food in both directions, from leaves to roots, fruits and growing parts.
Stomata are tiny pores in the leaf epidermis, each opened and closed by two guard cells. They allow exchange of gases and loss of water vapour (transpiration).
Ciliated epithelium in the windpipe sweeps mucus and trapped dust upwards. Smooth muscle in the intestine pushes food along without our control.
Blood transports materials: red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells fight infection and platelets help blood to clot.

ex.q: Think it through: A potted plant's leaves droop on a hot day, but recover in the evening after watering. Explain using tissues.
st: Leaves lose water vapour through stomata during transpiration, more on hot days.
If water is lost faster than xylem can bring it up, the cells lose water and the leaves droop.
After watering, roots absorb water and xylem carries it to the leaves.
The cells fill with water again and become firm, so the leaves stand up.
ex.a: Water lost through stomata was replaced when xylem brought fresh water to the leaves.

topics.rl: Gardeners water plants in the early morning or evening, when less water is lost through stomata.

topics.h: You run a full lap of the school ground and end up exactly where you started. You are tired, but how far have you really moved from the start? Physics gives two answers!
p: Motion is always described relative to a reference point. A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest relative to the train but in motion relative to the platform.
Distance is the total length of the path travelled. It has only magnitude, so it is a scalar quantity.
Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the starting point to the final point, in a stated direction. It has magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity.
Displacement can be zero even when distance is not, for example after one full round of a track.
The magnitude of displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled. The SI unit of both is the metre (m).

ex.q: Think it through: Kiran walks 6 km east from her house to a market and then 2 km west to a temple. Find the distance and the displacement.
st: Distance = total path = 6 km + 2 km = 8 km.
Displacement looks only at start and end points.
She ends 6 − 2 = 4 km east of her house.
So displacement = 4 km towards the east.
ex.a: Distance = 8 km; displacement = 4 km east.

topics.rl: An auto-rickshaw meter charges for distance travelled along the roads, while a map's straight 'as the crow flies' line shows displacement.

topics.h: The Vande Bharat express speeds up smoothly out of a station and slows down before the next one. How do we describe how fast it goes and how fast its speed changes?
p: Speed = distance ÷ time. Its SI unit is m/s. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time taken.
Velocity is speed in a stated direction: velocity = displacement ÷ time. It is a vector.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where u is the initial velocity and v is the final velocity. Its SI unit is m/s².
If velocity decreases, acceleration is negative (called deceleration or retardation). Uniform motion means equal distances in equal intervals of time.
In uniform circular motion the speed stays the same but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes and the motion is accelerated. To change km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18.

ex.q: Think it through: A car starts from rest and reaches 72 km/h in 10 s. What is its acceleration?
st: Change 72 km/h to m/s: 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
u = 0 (starts from rest), v = 20 m/s, t = 10 s.
a = 2 m/s².
ex.a: 2 m/s²

topics.rl: Speed limit boards on Indian highways, speedometers in buses and the cricket radar that shows how fast a fast bowler delivers the ball all measure speed.

topics.h: Before a cricket ball even lands, physics can tell you where it will land. For motion with uniform acceleration, three short equations do the job!
p: For uniform acceleration along a straight line: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², and v² = u² + 2as, where s is the displacement.
On a distance–time graph, a horizontal line means the object is at rest; a straight sloping line means uniform speed; the slope gives the speed.
On a velocity–time graph, a horizontal line means uniform velocity; a straight sloping line means uniform acceleration; the slope gives the acceleration.
The area under a velocity–time graph gives the displacement.
Always change units to m and s before using the equations.

ex.q: Think it through: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a uniform acceleration of −4 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?
st: u = 20 m/s, v = 0 (it stops), a = −4 m/s².
We do not know t, so use v² = u² + 2as.

topics.rl: Road safety engineers use these equations to work out braking distances and decide speed limits near schools.

topics.h: Your milkman calls his milk 'pure', but a chemist would call it a mixture! In science, 'pure' has a very special meaning.
p: A pure substance is made of only one kind of particle and has a fixed composition. Pure substances are elements or compounds.
An element cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions, for example oxygen, copper and mercury.

A compound is formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion by mass. Its properties are different from those of its elements. Water always has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.
A mixture has two or more substances that are not chemically combined. Its composition can vary, each component keeps its own properties, and it can be separated by physical methods.
A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout (salt water, air, brass). A heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts (sand in water, oil in water).

ex.q: Think it through: Iron filings and sulphur powder are mixed. Part of the mixture is then heated strongly by the teacher to form iron sulphide. How can a magnet show the difference?
st: In the unheated mixture, iron keeps its own properties.
So a magnet pulls the iron filings out of the mixture.
On heating, iron and sulphur combine chemically to form a new compound, iron sulphide.
The compound has new properties, and a magnet does not pull iron out of it.
ex.a: The magnet separates iron from the mixture but not from the compound iron sulphide.

topics.rl: Air, sea water, soil, brass utensils and even the steel of a kitchen spoon are all mixtures.

topics.h: Shine a torch through a glass of salt water and you see nothing special. Shine it through diluted milk and a glowing beam appears! What is different?
p: A solution is a homogeneous mixture. The substance that dissolves is the solute; the one it dissolves in is the solvent. In nimbu paani, sugar and salt are solutes and water is the solvent.
Concentration (mass by mass %) = mass of solute ÷ mass of solution × 100. A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature.
A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture whose particles can be seen, settle down on standing and can be separated by filtration, for example chalk powder in water.
A colloid looks homogeneous but is actually heterogeneous. Its particles are too small to see, do not settle and pass through filter paper, but they scatter light.
The scattering of a beam of light by colloid particles is the Tyndall effect. Milk, fog, smoke, butter, jelly and shaving cream are colloids.

ex.q: Think it through: Anu dissolves 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the concentration of the solution in mass by mass percentage?
st: Mass of solute = 20 g.
Mass of solution = solute + solvent = 20 + 180 = 200 g.
Concentration = 20 ÷ 200 × 100.
Concentration = 10%.
ex.a: 10% (mass by mass)

topics.rl: ORS for a child with loose motions is a solution; milk and curd are colloids; and the misty sunbeams seen in hill forests show the Tyndall effect.

topics.h: How does a dairy take the cream out of milk, and how do salt makers on the Gujarat coast get salt from the sea? Each mixture needs its own clever trick!
p: Evaporation removes a liquid and leaves the dissolved solid behind, as in getting salt from sea water. Crystallisation gives purer crystals than evaporating to dryness, because impurities stay in the remaining liquid.
Centrifugation spins a mixture very fast so heavier particles collect at the bottom. It separates cream from milk and is used in blood tests.

A separating funnel separates two liquids that do not mix, such as kerosene and water. Sublimation separates a substance that changes directly from solid to vapour, such as camphor, naphthalene or ammonium chloride, from one that does not.
Chromatography separates coloured parts of a mixture, such as dyes in ink, because they travel at different speeds up the paper.

Distillation separates two liquids that mix but have well-separated boiling points (acetone and water). Fractional distillation is used when boiling points are close, as in separating the gases of air or the parts of petroleum.

ex.q: Think it through: How would you separate a mixture of sand, common salt and camphor?
st: Camphor sublimes, so an adult heats the mixture gently under a funnel; camphor vapour collects on the cool funnel.
Add water to the remaining sand and salt and stir. Salt dissolves, sand does not.
Filter: sand stays on the filter paper.
Evaporate the filtrate (with adult help) to get the salt back.
ex.a: Sublimation for camphor, then dissolving and filtration for sand, then evaporation for salt.

topics.rl: Water treatment plants use sedimentation, loading with alum and filtration, and refineries use fractional distillation to get petrol, diesel and kerosene from crude oil.

topics.h: Why does a heavy almirah refuse to move until three people push together, and why does a rocket fly up by throwing gases down? Three laws explain it all!
p: A force is a push or a pull. Balanced forces cancel out and do not change motion; an unbalanced (net) force changes the speed or direction of motion.
First law: an object stays at rest, or keeps moving with uniform velocity in a straight line, unless an unbalanced force acts on it.
Second law: the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction of the force. This gives F = m × a.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N). 1 N is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².
Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they do not cancel each other.

ex.q: Think it through: What force is needed to give a 1000 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
st: Use the second law: F = m × a.
m = 1000 kg, a = 2 m/s².

topics.rl: ISRO's rockets push hot gases downwards at great speed, and by the third law the gases push the rocket upwards.

topics.h: Why do you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly, and why does a fielder pull back his hands while catching a hard cricket ball?
p: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.
Mass is the measure of inertia. A loaded truck has much more inertia than a bicycle, so it is harder to start or stop.
Momentum p = mass × velocity. It is a vector, and its SI unit is kg m/s. A parked car has zero momentum.
A force changes momentum. Taking more time to stop a moving object means a smaller force is needed. That is why a fielder pulls his hands back.
Law of conservation of momentum: when no external force acts, the total momentum of a system stays the same. A gun recoils backwards when a bullet is fired forwards.

ex.q: Think it through: A 0.02 kg bullet is fired from a 2 kg gun at 100 m/s. With what speed does the gun recoil?
st: Before firing, everything is at rest, so total momentum = 0.
Momentum of the bullet = 0.02 × 100 = 2 kg m/s forwards.
The gun must have 2 kg m/s backwards so the total stays 0.
Recoil speed = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 m/s.
ex.a: 1 m/s backwards

topics.rl: Seat belts, airbags and the sand pit in a long-jump event all increase the time taken to stop, which reduces the force on the body.

topics.h: The same force that makes a mango drop from a tree keeps the Moon going round the Earth. Isaac Newton realised it is all one force: gravitation!
p: Universal law of gravitation: every object attracts every other object with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G m₁m₂ ÷ d².
G is the universal gravitational constant, about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg². Because G is so small, the pull between everyday objects is too weak to notice.
Near the Earth's surface, all freely falling objects have the same acceleration due to gravity, g ≈ 9.8 m/s², if air resistance is ignored. g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator.
Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the force with which a planet pulls an object: W = m × g, measured in newtons.
On the Moon, g is about one-sixth of its value on the Earth, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much there. The Moon's pull is the main cause of tides.

ex.q: Think it through: Vikram's mass is 60 kg. What is his weight on the Earth, and what would his mass be on the Moon? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
st: Weight on the Earth = m × g = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.
Mass is the amount of matter in his body.
Going to the Moon does not change the amount of matter.
So his mass on the Moon is still 60 kg (but his weight would be about one-sixth of 588 N, about 98 N).
ex.a: Weight on the Earth = 588 N; mass on the Moon = 60 kg.

topics.rl: Chandrayaan-3's lander had to be guided down carefully to the Moon, whose gravity is much weaker than the Earth's, and fishermen along the coast plan their trips around tides caused by the Moon.

topics.h: You stand holding a heavy school bag for ten minutes and your arms ache. Yet a physicist says you did no work at all! What does 'work' really mean?
p: In science, work is done when a force moves an object. Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force: W = F × s.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J). 1 J of work is done when a force of 1 N moves an object by 1 m in its own direction.
No work is done if there is no displacement, or if the force is at right angles to the displacement. Work is negative when the force opposes the motion, like friction on a sliding box.
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t. Its SI unit is the watt (W); 1 W = 1 J/s and 1 kW = 1000 W.
Electrical energy is sold in kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = 1 'unit' = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

ex.q: Think it through: Ravi pushes a box with a force of 20 N and moves it 5 m along the floor in 10 s. How much work does he do, and what is his power?
st: The force and the displacement are in the same direction.
Power = work ÷ time = 100 ÷ 10.
Power = 10 W.
ex.a: Work = 100 J; power = 10 W.

topics.rl: Your family's electricity bill counts 'units', and every unit is 1 kWh of energy. A 1000 W geyser running for one hour uses 1 unit.

topics.h: Water stored high behind the Bhakra Nangal dam lights up homes in many states. How can water just sitting high up hold so much energy?
p: Energy is the capacity to do work. Its SI unit is the joule, the same as work.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large.
Potential energy is stored energy due to position or shape. Gravitational potential energy at height h is PE = mgh; a stretched rubber band or a bent bow has elastic potential energy.
Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes from one form to another. The total energy stays the same.
For a freely falling object (ignoring air resistance), potential energy turns into kinetic energy, but their sum, the mechanical energy, stays constant.

ex.q: Think it through: A 2 kg coconut falls from a height of 5 m. What is its potential energy at the top, and its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground? (Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance.)
st: PE at the top = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.
At the top it is at rest, so KE = 0.
As it falls, PE changes into KE, and the total stays 100 J.
Just before hitting the ground PE ≈ 0, so KE ≈ 100 J.
ex.a: PE at the top = 100 J; KE just before landing = 100 J.

topics.rl: Hydroelectric dams change the potential energy of stored water into electricity, and the fun of a swing comes from KE and PE swapping back and forth.

topics.h: How does a small child lift a heavy friend on a see-saw, and how is a heavy bucket raised from a village well with ease? Simple machines!
p: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The force we apply is the effort, and the weight lifted is the load.
Principle of the lever: load × load arm = effort × effort arm. Mechanical advantage (MA) = load ÷ effort.

First-class lever: fulcrum between effort and load (see-saw, scissors, beam balance). Second-class: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener). Third-class: effort between fulcrum and load (fire tongs, fishing rod, human forearm).
A single fixed pulley does not reduce the effort (MA = 1) but changes its direction, so you can pull down to lift up, as at a well or a flagpole.
A single movable pulley ideally has MA = 2, so the effort is half the load. Combinations of pulleys (block and tackle) are used in cranes.

ex.q: Think it through: A load of 200 N sits 0.5 m from the fulcrum of a crowbar. The effort is applied 2 m from the fulcrum on the other side. What effort is needed?
st: Principle of the lever: load × load arm = effort × effort arm.
100 = effort × 2.
Effort = 50 N, and MA = 200 ÷ 50 = 4.
ex.a: Effort = 50 N (MA = 4)

topics.rl: The hand pump in a village, a pair of scissors, the nutcracker (sarota) for supari and the crane at a construction site are all simple machines.

topics.h: Imagine firing tiny bullets at a sheet of tissue paper and a few of them bounce straight back at you! That shocking result revealed the nucleus.
p: Dalton (1808) imagined atoms as tiny indivisible balls. J.J. Thomson's discovery of the electron (1897) showed that atoms have smaller parts inside.
Thomson's model (1904): an atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon. The atom as a whole is neutral.
Rutherford's gold foil experiment: fast alpha particles were fired at a very thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, some were deflected and very few bounced back.

Rutherford's model (1911): the atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre and electrons revolving around it. But revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus, so this model could not explain why atoms are stable.
Bohr's model (1913): electrons revolve only in certain special orbits, or shells (K, L, M, N...), and do not radiate energy while in these orbits.

ex.q: Think it through: In Rutherford's experiment, why did very few alpha particles bounce back?
st: Alpha particles are positively charged and fast.
To bounce back, they must hit something positive, heavy and concentrated head-on.
Since only a very few bounced back, this positive, heavy part must be tiny.
So all the positive charge and almost all the mass are packed in a tiny nucleus.
ex.a: Only the very few particles that came close to the tiny, dense, positive nucleus were pushed back.

topics.rl: Scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai build on these atomic models when they work on nuclear energy and medicine.

topics.h: Carbon in your pencil and carbon used to date ancient wood are the same element, yet some of their atoms weigh more. How? Count the neutrons!
p: An atom has three main particles: the electron (charge −1, very small mass, about 1/1836 of a proton), the proton (charge +1, mass about 1 u) and the neutron (no charge, mass about 1 u). James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons move around it. In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons.
Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. So neutrons = A − Z.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14, or chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number, such as calcium-40 (Z = 20) and argon-40 (Z = 18). Some isotopes are useful: uranium-235 is a nuclear fuel and cobalt-60 is used to treat cancer.

ex.q: Think it through: Sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many protons, electrons and neutrons does a neutral sodium atom have?
st: Protons = atomic number = 11.
Neutral atom, so electrons = protons = 11.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11.
Neutrons = 12.
ex.a: 11 protons, 11 electrons and 12 neutrons.

topics.rl: Hospitals use radioactive isotopes for diagnosis and cancer treatment, and India's nuclear power plants use isotopes of uranium as fuel.

topics.h: Why is neon in glowing signboards so 'lazy' that it hardly reacts, while sodium reacts with water violently? It all depends on how electrons are arranged!
p: Electrons are arranged in shells K, L, M, N (n = 1, 2, 3, 4). The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n²: K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32.
Shells are filled step by step from the innermost one. For the first 18 elements, the outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons.
Examples: carbon (6) = 2, 4; oxygen (8) = 2, 6; sodium (11) = 2, 8, 1; chlorine (17) = 2, 8, 7; argon (18) = 2, 8, 8.
Electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons. An outer shell with 8 electrons (an octet), or 2 for helium, is stable, so noble gases hardly react.

Valency is the combining capacity of an atom. If valence electrons are 1 to 4, valency = valence electrons; if 5 to 8, valency = 8 − valence electrons. Sodium has valency 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3 and carbon 4.

ex.q: Think it through: Magnesium has atomic number 12. Write its electronic configuration and find its valency.
st: 12 electrons to place.
K shell takes 2, L shell takes 8: that uses 10.
The remaining 2 go into the M shell: 2, 8, 2.
Two valence electrons, which it can lose to get an octet, so valency = 2.
ex.a: 2, 8, 2; valency 2

topics.rl: Electronic configuration explains why table salt forms from sodium and chlorine, and why helium is used in balloons safely: it does not react.

topics.t: Atoms, molecules and the laws of chemical combination
topics.h: Burn a candle and it seems to vanish. But if you weighed the wax, the oxygen it uses and every bit of gas it gives off, the total mass would not change at all!
p: Law of conservation of mass (Lavoisier): mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
Law of constant proportions (Proust): a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass. Water from any source has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.

Dalton's atomic theory explained these laws: all matter is made of tiny atoms; atoms of one element are identical in mass and properties; atoms combine in small whole-number ratios; atoms are neither created nor destroyed in reactions. His idea that atoms are indivisible was later shown to be wrong.
Each element has a symbol, often from its English or Latin name: O for oxygen, Na for sodium (natrium), Fe for iron (ferrum), K for potassium (kalium).

A molecule is the smallest particle of an element or compound that can exist independently. Atomicity is the number of atoms in a molecule: helium (He) is monoatomic, O₂ diatomic, O₃ triatomic. Charged particles are ions: cations are positive and anions are negative.

ex.q: Think it through: 3 g of carbon burns completely in 8 g of oxygen. How much carbon dioxide is formed, and which law does this use?
st: Total mass of reactants = 3 g + 8 g = 11 g.
Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
So the mass of carbon dioxide = 11 g.
This is the law of conservation of mass.
ex.a: 11 g of carbon dioxide; law of conservation of mass.

topics.rl: Medicine makers rely on the law of constant proportions: a pure compound used in a tablet has the same elements in the same proportion by mass, whichever factory or country it comes from.

topics.h: An atom is far too tiny to weigh on any balance. So how do chemists say one oxygen atom is 16 times heavier than one hydrogen atom? They compare!
p: Atoms are too small to weigh directly, so we use relative masses. The standard is the carbon-12 atom.
One atomic mass unit (1 u) is exactly one-twelfth (1/12) of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
Common atomic masses: H = 1 u, C = 12 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, Na = 23 u, Mg = 24 u, S = 32 u, Cl = 35.5 u, Ca = 40 u.
Molecular mass = sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. For example, H₂O = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 u.
For ionic compounds such as NaCl we use the formula unit mass: 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 u.

ex.q: Think it through: Find the molecular mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄. (H = 1 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u)
st: Hydrogen: 2 atoms × 1 u = 2 u.
Sulphur: 1 atom × 32 u = 32 u.
Oxygen: 4 atoms × 16 u = 64 u.

topics.rl: Fertiliser makers calculate molecular masses to know how much nitrogen is in each bag of urea, so farmers know how much to use.

topics.t: Chemical formulae and the mole concept
topics.h: Chemists count atoms the way a shopkeeper counts eggs in dozens, but their 'dozen' is a giant number called a mole: about 602 billion trillion!
p: To write a formula, write the symbols (positive ion first), then cross over the valencies. Al (3) and O (2) give Al₂O₃; Mg (2) and Cl (1) give MgCl₂. Polyatomic ions with more than one unit go in brackets: Ca(OH)₂.
Common polyatomic ions: sulphate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, hydroxide OH⁻, ammonium NH₄⁺.
One mole of anything contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules or ions). This number is the Avogadro constant.
Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams; it equals the atomic or molecular mass in u. Water: 18 u, so its molar mass is 18 g.
Number of moles = given mass ÷ molar mass. Number of particles = number of moles × 6.022 × 10²³.

ex.q: Think it through: How many moles of water are in 36 g of water, and how many molecules is that?
st: Molar mass of H₂O = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 g.
Moles = 36 ÷ 18 = 2 mol.
Molecules = 2 × 6.022 × 10²³.
ex.a: 2 moles, which is 1.2044 × 10²⁴ molecules.

topics.rl: Chemists in medicine factories work in moles to make sure every tablet gets exactly the right number of medicine molecules.

topics.h: A tabla player strikes the same drum gently and then hard, on the edge and then in the centre. The beats change in loudness and pitch. What is changing in the sound wave?
p: Sound is produced by vibrating objects and needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
In air, sound travels as a longitudinal wave: the particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of the wave, forming compressions (crowded regions) and rarefactions (spread-out regions).
Frequency (f) is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Time period T = 1 ÷ f. Higher frequency gives a higher pitch.
Amplitude is the maximum disturbance of the particles from their normal position. Larger amplitude gives a louder sound.

Wave speed = frequency × wavelength (v = f × λ). Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases. Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz; lower is infrasound and higher is ultrasound.

ex.q: Think it through: A tuning fork vibrates at 170 Hz. If sound travels at 340 m/s in air, what is the wavelength of the sound?
st: Use v = f × λ, so λ = v ÷ f.
v = 340 m/s and f = 170 Hz.
λ = 2 m.
ex.a: 2 m

topics.rl: A flute and a sitar playing the same note sound different because of their quality (timbre), and doctors use the high frequencies of ultrasound to see inside the body.

topics.h: Shout 'Hello!' towards a big hill and the hill shouts back a moment later. Ships use the same trick, with sounds we cannot hear, to measure how deep the ocean is!
p: Sound reflects from hard surfaces. An echo is the reflected sound heard separately from the original sound.
Our brain keeps a sound for about 0.1 s, so an echo is heard distinctly only if it returns after at least 0.1 s. With sound at 340 m/s, the reflecting surface must be at least 17 m away.
Reverberation is the persistence of sound in a hall because of repeated reflections. It is reduced by curtains, carpets, cushioned seats and sound-absorbing panels.
SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) uses ultrasound. A ship sends ultrasound down, receives the echo from the sea bed and finds the depth d = (v × t) ÷ 2, since the sound goes down and comes back.
Bats and dolphins use echoes of ultrasound to find their way and catch prey. Doctors use ultrasound to make images of organs and of a baby in the womb.

ex.q: Think it through: A ship's SONAR receives an echo from the sea bed 4 s after sending a pulse. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, how deep is the sea?
st: Total distance travelled by sound = v × t = 1500 × 4 = 6000 m.
This is the distance down AND back up.
Depth = 3000 m.

topics.rl: Indian Navy ships and research ships use SONAR to map the sea bed, and fishermen use fish-finders that work in the same way.

topics.h: Your ear can pick up a whisper and a thunderclap, and it contains the smallest bone in your whole body, smaller than a grain of rice!
p: Outer ear: the pinna collects sound and sends it through the ear canal (auditory canal) to the eardrum.

Middle ear: the eardrum (tympanic membrane) vibrates with the sound. Three tiny bones, the hammer (malleus), anvil (incus) and stirrup (stapes), pass on and amplify these vibrations. The stirrup is the smallest bone in the human body.
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat and keeps the air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum.
Inner ear: the snail-shaped cochlea turns the vibrations into electrical signals, which the auditory nerve carries to the brain. The brain interprets them as sound.
Care for your ears: keep earphone volume low, take breaks, avoid very loud noise and never poke anything sharp into the ear.

ex.q: Think it through: While driving up a hill road to Shimla, Tanya's ears feel blocked and then 'pop' when she swallows. Why?
st: As the car climbs, the outside air pressure drops.
For a while, the air pressure in the middle ear is higher than outside, so the eardrum is pushed outwards and feels blocked.
Swallowing opens the Eustachian tube, which joins the middle ear to the throat.
Air moves through it, the pressures become equal and the ear 'pops'.
ex.a: The Eustachian tube opened and equalised the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum.

topics.rl: Audiologists test hearing with sounds of different frequencies, and hearing aids amplify sounds for people with hearing loss.

topics.h: Leave a potato in a dark corner for a few weeks and tiny shoots pop out of its 'eyes'. Plant it, and you get new potato plants without any seeds at all!
p: Reproduction is the making of new individuals of the same kind. In asexual reproduction a single parent produces offspring, without gametes.
Fission: Amoeba and bacteria split into two (binary fission); the malaria parasite Plasmodium splits into many at once (multiple fission).

Budding: a small outgrowth (bud) grows on the parent and develops into a new individual, as in Hydra and yeast. Fragmentation: a filament of Spirogyra breaks into pieces and each piece grows into a new one. Regeneration: a cut piece of Planaria can grow into a whole new animal.
Spore formation: bread mould (Rhizopus) makes spores in sporangia, which grow into new moulds in moist, warm places.

Vegetative propagation: new plants grow from roots, stems or leaves, such as potato eyes, ginger rhizomes, onion bulbs, Bryophyllum leaf buds and rose stem cuttings. Offspring of asexual reproduction are nearly identical to the parent.

ex.q: Think it through: A farmer wants all his new mango trees to give fruit exactly as sweet as his best tree. Should he grow them from seeds or by grafting? Why?
st: Seeds come from sexual reproduction and combine traits from two parents.
So trees from seeds may give fruit that is different from the parent tree.
Grafting is vegetative propagation, a form of asexual reproduction.
Grafted trees carry the same traits as the parent, so the fruit will be the same.
ex.a: Grafting, because asexually produced plants are nearly identical to the parent.

topics.rl: Nurseries grow roses from cuttings and mangoes by grafting, and farmers plant sugarcane from stem pieces instead of seeds.

topics.h: A bee buzzing from one sunflower to another is doing an important job without knowing it: helping the plants make seeds!
p: The flower is the reproductive part of a flowering plant. The stamen is the male part: an anther (which makes pollen grains) on a filament. The pistil (carpel) is the female part: stigma, style and ovary, which contains ovules.

Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma. Self-pollination happens within the same flower or plant; cross-pollination happens between flowers of different plants of the same kind.
Pollen is carried by wind, water, insects and birds. Bright, scented flowers with nectar usually attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make large amounts of light pollen.
Fertilisation: a pollen tube grows from the pollen grain down the style into the ovule, and a male gamete fuses with the female gamete (egg) to form a zygote.
After fertilisation, the zygote grows into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit. Petals and stamens usually wither and fall.

ex.q: Think it through: A mango flower has been pollinated and fertilised. What will each part become?
st: Inside the ovule, the zygote divides to form the embryo, the baby plant.
The ovule develops into the seed (the guthli) with the embryo inside.
The ovary swells and ripens into the fruit, the juicy mango.
The petals and stamens dry up and fall off.
ex.a: Zygote → embryo, ovule → seed, ovary → fruit.

topics.rl: Farmers keep bee boxes near mustard and sunflower fields because bees improve pollination and the harvest of seeds.

topics.h: Every frog, every peacock and every person began life as a single tiny cell. How can one cell grow into a whole animal?
p: In sexual reproduction two parents produce gametes: the male gamete is the sperm and the female gamete is the egg (ovum). Their fusion is called fertilisation.
Fertilisation forms a single cell, the zygote. It divides again and again to form an embryo, which grows into a new individual.
Internal fertilisation happens inside the female's body, as in humans, cows, dogs and hens. External fertilisation happens outside, usually in water, as in frogs and most fish.
Animals that give birth to young ones are viviparous (humans, cows, dogs). Animals that lay eggs are oviparous (hens, frogs, turtles). In humans, the embryo develops inside the mother's uterus.

Some animals change form as they grow, called metamorphosis: a frog goes from egg to tadpole to adult. Sexual reproduction mixes features of two parents, which gives variation and helps a species survive changes.

ex.q: Think it through: Frogs lay hundreds of eggs, but a cow usually gives birth to only one calf at a time. Why might frogs need so many eggs?
st: Frogs have external fertilisation in water.
Many eggs and sperm are carried away by water, eaten or never meet.
The eggs and tadpoles are not protected inside the mother's body.
So frogs lay many eggs to make sure that at least some survive to become adults.
ex.a: With external fertilisation and no protection inside the body, many eggs are lost, so frogs lay large numbers.

topics.rl: India is one of the world's major silk producers, and silk farmers (sericulturists) rear silkworms through their life cycle of egg, larva, pupa and moth.

topics.ch: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
topics.t: Why and how we classify living things
topics.h: India is home to tigers, peacocks, neem trees, tiny bacteria in curd and thousands of kinds of insects. How can anyone study so many living things? By sorting them into groups!
p: Classification is grouping organisms by their similarities and differences. It makes the huge variety of life easier to study and shows how organisms are related.

Important features used for classifying: is the cell prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Is the organism unicellular or multicellular? Does it make its own food (autotroph) or depend on others (heterotroph)? Does it have a cell wall?
Organisms are arranged in a hierarchy of levels: Kingdom → Phylum (Division for plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
As we go down from kingdom to species, groups get smaller and members share more and more features.
A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. It is the basic unit of classification.

ex.q: Think it through: A neem tree and a mushroom both grow out of the ground and do not move. Why are they placed in different kingdoms?
st: Look at the mode of nutrition.
The neem tree has chlorophyll and makes its own food by photosynthesis: it is an autotroph.
The mushroom has no chlorophyll and absorbs food from dead and decaying matter: it is a heterotroph.
Their cell walls also differ: cellulose in neem, chitin in mushroom. So neem is in Plantae and mushroom is in Fungi.
ex.a: They differ in nutrition (autotroph vs heterotroph) and cell-wall material, so neem is a plant and mushroom is a fungus.

topics.rl: The Botanical Survey of India and the Zoological Survey of India identify and classify the plants and animals of our country.

topics.ch: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
topics.h: A mango is 'aam' in Hindi, 'maavu' in Kannada and 'amba' in Marathi. But scientists everywhere call it Mangifera indica. One name for the whole world!
p: Carl Linnaeus, a Swedish scientist of the 18th century, introduced binomial nomenclature, a two-part scientific name for every species.
The first part is the genus name and the second part is the species name, for example Homo sapiens (humans) and Panthera tigris (tiger).
Rules: the genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter. In print the name is in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately.
Scientific names avoid confusion, because local names differ from place to place and language to language.
Indian examples: Azadirachta indica (neem), Mangifera indica (mango), Pavo cristatus (Indian peafowl), Panthera leo (lion), Ficus benghalensis (banyan).

ex.q: Think it through: A student writes the scientific name of the tiger as 'panthera Tigris'. What is wrong, and what is the correct form?
st: The first word is the genus, which must start with a capital letter: Panthera.
The second word is the species, which must start with a small letter: tigris.
In print the whole name is in italics; when handwritten, each word is underlined separately.
Correct form: Panthera tigris.
ex.a: The capitals are swapped; it should be Panthera tigris.

topics.rl: Forest officers, doctors and scientists from different countries use scientific names so that everyone knows exactly which plant or animal is meant.

topics.ch: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
topics.h: A bacterium in curd, an Amoeba in a pond, a mushroom after the monsoon rain, a lotus and a tiger: one representative from each of the five kingdoms!
p: In 1969 Robert Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. It is based on cell type, body organisation and mode of nutrition.
Monera: prokaryotic and unicellular. Some make their own food, others do not. Examples: bacteria and cyanobacteria (blue-green algae).
Protista: unicellular eukaryotes. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena and diatoms.
Fungi: eukaryotic heterotrophs, mostly saprophytes that absorb food from dead and decaying matter. Their cell walls contain chitin. Examples: yeast, mushrooms, bread mould (Rhizopus) and Penicillium.
Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls and chlorophyll; they are autotrophs. Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall; they are heterotrophs.

ex.q: Think it through: A newly found organism is many-celled, has eukaryotic cells with no cell wall and eats other organisms. Which kingdom does it belong to?
st: Eukaryotic cells rule out Monera.
Many-celled rules out Protista (single-celled eukaryotes).
No cell wall rules out Fungi and Plantae, which have cell walls.
Eating other organisms (heterotroph) fits Animalia.
ex.a: Animalia

topics.rl: Penicillium, a fungus, gave us the antibiotic penicillin, and cyanobacteria help fix nitrogen in paddy fields, which supports rice crops.

topics.ch: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
topics.h: When a volcano erupts, ash shoots into the air, lava covers the land, rivers get blocked and animals run away. One event touches every part of the Earth system at once!
p: Scientists study the Earth as a system of connected parts called spheres. A change in one sphere affects the others.

Lithosphere: the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth, including rocks, soil and mountains. Hydrosphere: all the water on Earth, in oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater and ice. About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, and most of it is salty ocean water.

Atmosphere: the layer of air around the Earth, mostly nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%), with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour. Weather happens in the lowest layer (troposphere); the ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays.
Biosphere: all living things and the parts of land, water and air where they live. The frozen parts of the hydrosphere, such as glaciers and ice caps, are called the cryosphere.
The Sun is the main source of energy for processes at the Earth's surface, such as winds, the water cycle and photosynthesis. Heat from inside the Earth drives volcanoes and earthquakes.

ex.q: Think it through: Trees on a hill slope in Uttarakhand are cut down. How can this one change affect the other spheres?
st: Biosphere: trees and the animals living in them are lost.
Lithosphere: without roots to hold it, soil is washed away during heavy rain, and landslides become more likely.
Hydrosphere: the washed-away soil makes rivers muddy and can cause flooding downstream.
Atmosphere: fewer trees take in carbon dioxide, so more of it stays in the air.
ex.a: Cutting trees changes the biosphere, which then affects soil (lithosphere), rivers (hydrosphere) and air (atmosphere).

topics.rl: ISRO's Earth-observation satellites monitor forests, glaciers, oceans and clouds, helping India plan for floods, droughts and cyclones.

topics.ch: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
topics.h: The water in your glass may once have fallen as rain on the Himalayas, and the carbon in your roti may once have been in a dinosaur's breath! Matter on Earth keeps moving in cycles.
p: Biogeochemical cycles move matter between living things (bio) and the rocks, water and air of the Earth (geo). Matter is recycled again and again, while energy from the Sun flows through the system in one direction.

Water cycle: the Sun's heat causes evaporation from water bodies and transpiration from leaves. The vapour cools and condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation (rain, snow, hail), then flows as runoff or soaks into the ground as groundwater.

Carbon cycle: plants take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. Respiration, decomposition and the burning of fuels return carbon dioxide to the air. Oceans dissolve carbon dioxide, and fossil fuels store carbon from ancient life.

Nitrogen cycle: plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, such as Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes (gram, peas, moong), and lightning convert it into compounds. Nitrifying bacteria form nitrates, which plants absorb to make proteins. Denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen gas to the air.
Oxygen cycle: photosynthesis releases oxygen; respiration, burning and decomposition use it up.

ex.q: Think it through: Farmers often grow moong or gram after a wheat crop. Why does this help the next crop?
st: Moong and gram are legumes.
Their root nodules contain Rhizobium bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air.
This adds nitrogen compounds to the soil.
The next crop gets more nitrogen for making proteins, so less chemical fertiliser is needed.
ex.a: Legumes add fixed nitrogen to the soil through Rhizobium in their root nodules.

topics.rl: Composting kitchen waste returns carbon and nitrogen to the soil, and rainwater harvesting puts water back into the ground as part of the water cycle.

topics.ch: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
topics.h: Shimla stays cool even in May, while Delhi bakes in the heat. Mumbai rarely gets very cold. Why do different places have such different climates?
p: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place for a short time, such as today's temperature, rainfall, humidity and wind. Climate is the average pattern of weather of a place over many years.

Climate depends on latitude, altitude (height above sea level), distance from the sea and winds. Hill stations are cooler because temperature falls with altitude; places near the sea have milder climates.
India's climate is shaped by the monsoon. The south-west monsoon, from about June to September, brings most of India's yearly rainfall.
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap heat in the atmosphere. This natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough for life.

Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests add extra greenhouse gases, which causes global warming and climate change: melting glaciers, rising sea levels and more extreme weather. Using solar energy, saving electricity, planting trees and using public transport help.

ex.q: Think it through: Mumbai and Delhi are both large cities, but Delhi has much hotter summers and colder winters. Why?
st: Mumbai is on the coast, right next to the Arabian Sea.
Water heats up and cools down more slowly than land.
So the sea keeps Mumbai's temperatures moderate all year.
Delhi is far from the sea, so it has extreme summers and winters.
ex.a: Mumbai's nearness to the sea moderates its climate; Delhi, far inland, has extremes.

topics.rl: Solar parks in Rajasthan and Gujarat and rooftop solar panels on homes help India produce electricity without adding carbon dioxide.

qa.q: Arjun says, "Tulsi plants kept in sunlight will grow taller than tulsi plants kept in shade." What is this statement?
qa.e: It is a possible explanation that can be tested by an experiment, so it is a hypothesis. It becomes a conclusion only after the evidence is collected.

qa.q: Priya tests how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls. What is the dependent variable?
qa.e: The dependent variable is the result you measure. Priya changes the ramp height and measures the distance rolled.

qa.q: To test whether more water makes moong seedlings grow faster, which of these must be kept the same for all pots?
qa.a: The amount of sunlight each pot gets
qa.e: Sunlight is a controlled variable: if it differs, you cannot tell whether water or light caused the change. Water is the variable being changed, while height and number of leaves are results that are measured.

qa.q: Why do scientists repeat an experiment several times?
qa.a: To make the results reliable and spot errors
qa.e: Repeating trials shows whether the results are consistent and reduces the effect of chance errors.

qa.q: The results of Kabir's experiment do not support his hypothesis. What should he do?
qa.a: Revise the hypothesis and test again
qa.e: Evidence decides. A hypothesis that does not fit the data is revised or replaced and then tested again. Data must never be changed to fit an idea.

qa.q: Which of these questions can be answered by a scientific experiment?
qa.a: Does sugar dissolve faster in warm water than in cold water?
qa.e: Dissolving time can be measured and compared. The other questions are matters of personal opinion and cannot be measured.

qa.q: Which statement is an observation rather than an inference?
qa.e: A smell is noticed directly with the senses, so it is an observation. The other options are explanations we guess from it.

qa.q: National Science Day is celebrated in India on 28 February. Which discovery does it mark?
qa.e: C.V. Raman announced the Raman effect, about how light is scattered, on 28 February 1928. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.

qa.q: Why is a globe called a model of the Earth?
qa.a: It is a smaller, simplified copy that shows the Earth's main features
qa.e: A model is a simplified representation. A globe keeps the shape and positions of continents and oceans but leaves out most details.

qa.q: What makes a scientific model useful?
qa.a: It explains observations and makes predictions that can be tested
qa.e: A model earns trust when its predictions match observations. Testable predictions are its main strength.

qa.q: A model predicts that a ball will land 5 m away, but careful repeated measurements show 8 m. What should scientists do?
qa.e: When reliable evidence disagrees with a prediction, the model has to be improved or replaced.

qa.q: Which of these is a mathematical model?
qa.e: A mathematical model uses an equation to describe and predict. The other three are physical models or diagrams.

qa.q: A school chart shows the Sun and planets in a row on one sheet. What is a limitation of this model?
qa.a: Its sizes and distances are not to scale
qa.e: Real distances between planets are enormous compared with their sizes, so a chart cannot show both to scale on one sheet.

qa.q: Which Indian organisation issues official weather forecasts and cyclone warnings using computer models?
qa.e: IMD is India's national weather agency. It runs weather models and issues forecasts and warnings.

qa.q: Ravi's model says, "Heavier objects sink in water." A large wooden log floats. What does this show?
qa.a: The model is incomplete and needs to be improved
qa.e: A heavy log floating disagrees with the prediction, so the model needs improving. Floating depends on density, not on weight alone.

qa.q: Which statement about scientific models is correct?
qa.a: A model can be useful even if it is not perfect
qa.e: All models simplify. They are useful as long as they explain and predict well enough for their purpose.

qa.q: Your stride is about 0.5 m long. Roughly how many steps will you take to walk 1 km?
qa.e: 1 km = 1000 m. Number of steps = 1000 ÷ 0.5 = 2000.

qa.q: Which is the best estimate of the height of a classroom door?
qa.e: A door is a little taller than an adult, so about 2 m is sensible. 20 m would be as tall as a six-storey building.

qa.q: If you sleep 8 hours every night, about how many hours do you sleep in a year of 365 days?
qa.e: 8 hours × 365 nights = 2920 hours, about one-third of all the hours in a year.

qa.q: How is 3 000 000 written in scientific notation?
qa.e: Move the decimal point 6 places to get 3. The first number must be at least 1 and less than 10, so it is 3 × 10⁶.

qa.q: How many SI base units are there?
qa.e: The 7 SI base units are the metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.

qa.q: If each person uses about 100 litres of water a day, roughly how much water does a family of 4 use in a week?
qa.e: Per day the family uses 100 × 4 = 400 litres. In 7 days that is 400 × 7 = 2800 litres.

qa.q: Which number is written correctly in scientific notation?
qa.e: All four equal 4500, but only 4.5 × 10³ has a first number that is at least 1 and less than 10.

qa.q: Which is the SI unit of time?
qa.e: The second is the SI base unit of time. Minutes, hours and days are commonly used but are not SI base units.

qa.q: Who first observed and named 'cells' while looking at a thin slice of cork?
qa.e: Robert Hooke saw box-like compartments in cork in 1665 and called them cells.

qa.q: In which year did Robert Hooke observe cells in cork?
qa.e: Hooke published his observations of cork cells in 1665 in his book Micrographia.

qa.q: Who was the first to see free-living cells in pond water?
qa.e: In 1674 Leeuwenhoek used his improved lenses to see tiny living cells moving in pond water.

qa.q: Which scientist stated that all cells arise from pre-existing cells?
qa.e: Rudolf Virchow added this idea to the cell theory in 1855.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a part of the cell theory?
qa.a: All cells have a cell wall
qa.e: Animal cells have no cell wall, so this cannot be a rule for all cells. The other three are the ideas of the cell theory.

qa.q: What did Robert Brown discover in 1831?
qa.e: Robert Brown observed and described the nucleus in plant cells.

qa.q: Schleiden studied plants and Schwann studied animals. What did their combined work show?
qa.a: Plants and animals are made of cells
qa.e: Together they showed that both plants and animals are built from cells, which became the cell theory.

qa.q: Why are microscopes needed to study most cells?
qa.a: Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye
qa.e: Most cells are only a few micrometres across, far smaller than the eye can see, so a lens is needed to magnify them.

qa.q: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
qa.e: Mitochondria release energy from food and store it as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.

qa.q: Which organelle packages materials made in the cell and sends them to their destinations?
qa.e: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials, many of which come from the ER.

qa.q: Lysosomes are called 'suicide bags'. Why?
qa.a: If the cell is damaged they can burst and their enzymes digest the cell
qa.e: Lysosomes are full of powerful digestive enzymes. When a cell is badly damaged, they may burst and digest their own cell.

qa.q: Where in the cell are proteins made?
qa.e: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis. Many are attached to rough ER.

qa.q: Which part of the cell allows some substances to pass but stops others?
qa.e: The cell membrane is selectively permeable. It controls what enters and leaves the cell.

qa.q: The cell wall of a plant cell is mainly made of
qa.e: Plant cell walls are made mostly of cellulose, which gives strength and shape. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls.

qa.q: Slices of cucumber sprinkled with salt become watery after some time. Why?
qa.a: Water moves out of the cucumber cells by osmosis
qa.e: The salty layer outside has less water than the cells, so water moves out of the cells across their membranes by osmosis.

qa.q: Why are the cells of a spinach leaf green?
qa.a: They contain chloroplasts with the pigment chlorophyll
qa.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that traps sunlight for photosynthesis.

qa.q: Which of these organisms is unicellular?
qa.e: Amoeba is made of just one cell that carries out all life processes. The others are multicellular.

qa.q: Which of these is a multicellular organism?
qa.e: Hydra is a small animal made of many cells. Paramecium, Chlamydomonas and yeast are single-celled.

qa.q: What is the main advantage of cells being specialised in a multicellular organism?
qa.a: Different jobs are shared, so the body works efficiently
qa.e: Division of labour lets each type of cell do its job very well, such as muscle cells contracting and nerve cells carrying messages.

qa.q: What does a prokaryotic cell lack?
qa.e: In prokaryotes the genetic material lies in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane. They do have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.

qa.q: Which organism has prokaryotic cells?
qa.e: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Amoeba and yeast are single-celled but eukaryotic, with a true nucleus.

qa.q: In a unicellular organism, who performs life processes such as feeding, respiration and excretion?
qa.e: A unicellular organism has only one cell, so that one cell must do every life process.

qa.q: Which organism changes its shape and moves using pseudopodia?
qa.e: Amoeba pushes out finger-like pseudopodia to move and to capture food. Paramecium moves using tiny hair-like cilia.

qa.q: Which of these is a eukaryotic cell?
qa.e: Onion cells, like all plant cells, have a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane. Bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes.

qa.q: Which tissue makes a root or a shoot grow longer at its tip?
qa.e: Apical meristem is present at the growing tips of roots and stems and increases their length.

qa.q: The trunk of a neem tree becomes thicker every year. Which tissue causes this?
qa.e: Lateral meristem, also called cambium, divides to increase the girth of stems and roots.

qa.q: The husk of a coconut is made of which tissue?
qa.e: Coconut husk has sclerenchyma fibres: dead cells with thick, lignified walls that make it hard.

qa.q: Which tissue helps aquatic plants like water hyacinth float?
qa.e: Aerenchyma is parenchyma with large air cavities that give buoyancy.

qa.q: Which tissue lets the leaf stalk bend in the wind without breaking?
qa.e: Collenchyma cells are living, with walls thickened only at the corners, giving support with flexibility.

qa.q: Which tissue carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves?
qa.e: Xylem, made of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, carries water and dissolved minerals upwards.

qa.q: Which tissue carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant?
qa.e: Phloem, made of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres, carries food.

qa.q: Desert plants have a thick waxy cuticle on their epidermis. What is its main use?
qa.e: The waxy cuticle is water-resistant, so it cuts down water loss in hot, dry places.

qa.q: Which tissue joins a muscle to a bone?
qa.e: Tendons are strong fibrous connective tissue joining muscles to bones.

qa.q: Which tissue joins one bone to another bone?
qa.e: Ligaments are elastic connective tissue that hold bones together at joints.

qa.q: The inner lining of the mouth is made of which tissue?
qa.e: Thin, flat squamous epithelial cells line the mouth and blood vessels.

qa.q: Why is blood called a connective tissue?
qa.a: It has cells in a fluid matrix and connects body parts by transport
qa.e: Blood has RBCs, WBCs and platelets in liquid plasma, and it carries materials between all parts of the body.

qa.q: Which tissue stores fat below the skin and helps insulate the body?
qa.e: Adipose tissue cells are filled with fat globules, which store energy and reduce heat loss.

qa.q: Which muscle is involuntary, has branched cells and contracts rhythmically throughout life?
qa.e: Cardiac (heart) muscle cells are branched and cylindrical and keep contracting rhythmically all through life.

qa.q: Which part of a neuron carries a nerve impulse away from the cell body?
qa.e: The axon is the long fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites receive impulses.

qa.q: The bendable part of your outer ear is supported by
qa.e: Cartilage is a firm but flexible connective tissue that supports the ear and the tip of the nose.

qa.q: Which pair of cells opens and closes a stoma?
qa.e: Each stoma is bordered by two kidney-shaped guard cells that change shape to open or close the pore.

qa.q: Which two jobs do stomata perform?
qa.e: Carbon dioxide and oxygen pass through stomata, and water vapour escapes through them during transpiration.

qa.q: Sugar made in mango leaves reaches the ripening fruit and the roots. Which tissue carries it, and in which direction?
qa.e: Phloem carries food from the leaves to wherever it is needed, up or down. Xylem carries water only upwards.

qa.q: Food keeps moving through your intestine even when you are asleep. Which tissue does this?
qa.e: Smooth muscle in the wall of the alimentary canal contracts on its own, without conscious control.

qa.q: What is the job of the ciliated epithelium lining the windpipe?
qa.a: To sweep mucus and trapped dust out of the airway
qa.e: The cilia beat together and move dust-trapping mucus up and away from the lungs.

qa.q: Which part of blood helps a small cut stop bleeding by forming a clot?
qa.e: Platelets help blood to clot and seal the wound.

qa.q: Why are bones hard and strong?
qa.a: Their matrix contains calcium and phosphorus compounds
qa.e: Bone cells sit in a hard matrix made of calcium and phosphorus compounds, giving the body a strong frame.

qa.q: Why are sclerenchyma cells good at making plant parts hard?
qa.a: They have thick walls hardened with lignin
qa.e: Lignin is a cementing substance that thickens and hardens the walls of sclerenchyma cells.

qa.q: Neha runs exactly one round of a 400 m circular track and stops at the start line. What are her distance and displacement?
qa.e: She covered a path of 400 m, but she ended where she began, so her displacement is zero.

qa.q: Aman walks 3 m east and then 4 m north. What is the magnitude of his displacement?
qa.e: The two walks are at right angles, so the straight line from start to end is the hypotenuse: √(3² + 4²) = 5 m.

qa.q: Kiran walks 6 km east and then 2 km west. What is the magnitude of her displacement?
qa.e: The walks are in opposite directions, so she ends 6 − 2 = 4 km east of her start.

qa.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
qa.e: Displacement has both magnitude and direction. Distance, time and mass have only magnitude.

qa.q: A boy walks along a curved road from his house to school. Compared with the distance, the magnitude of his displacement is
qa.e: A curved path is longer than the straight line joining its ends, so displacement is less than distance.

qa.q: Riya is sitting in a moving train. Relative to which of these is she at rest?
qa.a: The seat she is sitting on
qa.e: Her position does not change relative to the seat, which moves with her. Relative to the ground, she is moving.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of displacement?
qa.e: Displacement is a length, so its SI unit is the metre.

qa.q: Sameer climbs 3 floors up and then comes back down to the ground floor. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: His displacement is zero but the distance is not
qa.e: He ended at his starting point, so displacement is zero, but he did travel along the stairs, so distance is not zero.

qa.q: A bus covers 120 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed in km/h?
qa.e: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h.

qa.q: A train runs at 72 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?
A car starts from rest and reaches 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
A motorbike slows from 15 m/s to 5 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
qa.e: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (5 − 15) ÷ 5 = −2 m/s². The minus sign shows it is slowing down.

qa.q: Why is a child on a merry-go-round turning at a steady speed said to be accelerating?
qa.a: Because the direction of motion keeps changing
qa.e: Velocity includes direction. In circular motion the direction changes every moment, so the velocity changes and there is acceleration.

qa.q: What is the main difference between speed and velocity?
qa.a: Velocity has a direction, speed does not
qa.e: Both are measured in m/s, but velocity is a vector with a direction, while speed is a scalar.

qa.q: Rohan cycles 10 km to his tuition centre and comes back home by the same road. What is his average velocity for the whole trip, in km/h?
qa.e: He ends where he started, so his total displacement is zero, and average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 0.

qa.q: A car moves on a straight road with a constant velocity of 15 m/s. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
qa.e: Acceleration is the change in velocity per second. If velocity does not change, acceleration is zero.

qa.q: A train starts from rest with an acceleration of 2 m/s². What is its velocity after 10 s, in m/s?
The same train (starting from rest, a = 2 m/s²) travels how far in those 10 s?
qa.e: s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½ × 2 × 10² = 100 m.

qa.q: A car at 20 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −4 m/s². What distance does it cover before it stops?
On a distance–time graph, a horizontal straight line shows that the object is
qa.e: A horizontal line means the distance is not changing as time passes, so the object is not moving.

qa.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the
qa.e: Slope = change in velocity ÷ time, which is the definition of acceleration.

qa.q: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give?
qa.e: Velocity × time = displacement, so the area between the graph and the time axis gives the displacement.

qa.q: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 10 m/s at t = 5 s. What is the displacement in these 5 s?
qa.e: The area under the line is a triangle: ½ × base × height = ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m.

qa.q: Which equation would you use to find the final velocity when you know u, a and s, but not t?
qa.e: v² = u² + 2as links v, u, a and s without needing the time.

qa.q: Which of these is a compound?
qa.e: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Oxygen is an element; air and brass are mixtures.

qa.q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
qa.e: Sugar spreads evenly through the water, so every part has the same composition.

qa.q: Which property belongs to a compound but NOT to a mixture?
qa.a: Its elements are present in a fixed ratio by mass
qa.e: A compound always has a fixed composition. The other three statements describe mixtures.

qa.q: Brass is best described as
qa.a: a homogeneous mixture (alloy) of copper and zinc
qa.e: Brass is an alloy. Its metals are evenly mixed but not chemically combined, and its composition can vary.

qa.q: Which statement describes an element?
qa.a: It cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical reactions
qa.e: An element is the simplest form of matter; chemical reactions cannot split it into simpler substances.

qa.q: The milkman says his milk is 'pure'. For a scientist, milk is
qa.e: Milk contains water, fats, proteins, sugar and minerals that are not chemically combined, so it is a mixture.

qa.q: Why is air called a mixture and not a compound?
qa.a: Its composition can vary and each gas keeps its own properties
qa.e: Air has varying amounts of gases such as water vapour, and each gas keeps its own properties, so it is a mixture.

qa.q: Hydrogen and oxygen combine in a fixed mass ratio to form water. What is this ratio (hydrogen : oxygen)?
qa.e: In water, 1 g of hydrogen always combines with 8 g of oxygen. The 2 : 1 ratio is the number of atoms, not the mass.

qa.q: Anu dissolves 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the concentration in mass by mass %?
qa.e: Concentration = solute ÷ solution × 100 = 20 ÷ (20 + 180) × 100 = 10%.

qa.q: Which of these will show the Tyndall effect when a torch beam passes through it?
qa.e: Milk is a colloid, and its particles are big enough to scatter light. Particles in true solutions are too small to scatter light.
