qa.q: Chalk powder stirred in water settles at the bottom after some time. This mixture is a
qa.e: Suspension particles are large enough to be seen and they settle on standing.

qa.q: In a glass of sugar sharbat, which is the solvent?
qa.e: The solvent is the substance in which the solute dissolves. Sugar dissolves in water, so water is the solvent.

qa.q: What is a saturated solution?
qa.a: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature
qa.e: When a solution holds as much solute as it can at a given temperature, it is saturated.

qa.q: Fog is a colloid in which
qa.a: tiny water droplets are dispersed in air
qa.e: In fog, the dispersed phase is liquid water and the dispersion medium is air (a gas). Such a colloid is an aerosol.

qa.q: Which mixture can be separated by filtration?
qa.e: Chalk particles in a suspension are big enough to be trapped by filter paper. Solution and colloid particles pass through.

qa.q: Sunbeams entering a misty forest look like bright streaks. Why?
qa.a: Mist droplets scatter the light (Tyndall effect)
qa.e: Mist is a colloid. Its tiny droplets scatter sunlight, making the path of the light visible.

qa.q: Which method separates cream from milk?
qa.e: Spinning the milk very fast separates the lighter cream from the rest of the milk.

qa.q: How would you separate a mixture of kerosene and water?
qa.e: Kerosene and water do not mix and form two layers. A separating funnel lets the lower water layer drain out first.

qa.q: Which method separates camphor from common salt?
qa.e: Camphor turns directly into vapour on gentle heating and can be collected on a cool surface; salt does not sublime.

qa.q: Which technique shows that black ink is a mixture of different dyes?
qa.e: In paper chromatography, each dye travels a different distance up the paper, so the colours separate.

qa.q: Salt makers along the coast of Gujarat obtain salt from sea water mainly by
qa.e: Sea water is let into shallow pans, the Sun evaporates the water, and salt is left behind.

qa.q: Which method is used to separate the different gases from air?
qa.e: Air is cooled to become a liquid, then warmed slowly; gases like nitrogen, argon and oxygen boil off at different temperatures.

qa.q: Why is crystallisation better than evaporating to dryness for getting pure copper sulphate?
qa.a: Soluble impurities stay in the liquid, and the solid is not overheated
qa.e: In crystallisation, pure crystals form while impurities remain dissolved. Evaporating to dryness leaves impurities mixed in and can damage some solids.

qa.q: Acetone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (100 °C) mix completely. Which method separates them?
qa.e: They mix, so a funnel will not work. Their boiling points are far apart, so distillation boils off the acetone first.

qa.q: A force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg trolley. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
What force, in newtons, is needed to give a 1000 kg car an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
Which statement is Newton's first law of motion?
qa.a: An object stays at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it
qa.e: The first law describes inertia: objects keep their state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts.

qa.q: You push a wall with a force of 50 N. What does the wall do?
qa.e: By the third law, the wall exerts an equal and opposite force of 50 N on your hands.

qa.q: Action and reaction forces are equal and opposite. Why don't they cancel each other?
qa.e: Forces cancel only when they act on the same body. Action acts on one body and reaction on the other.

qa.q: How does a rocket move upwards?
qa.a: Hot gases pushed down by the rocket push the rocket up
qa.e: This is the third law: the rocket pushes gases down (action) and the gases push the rocket up (reaction). It works even in space with no air.

qa.q: In a tug of war, both teams pull the rope with 500 N in opposite directions. What happens?
qa.a: The rope does not move, because the forces are balanced
qa.e: Equal and opposite forces on the same rope are balanced, so the net force is zero and the rope stays still.

qa.q: What is 1 newton?
qa.a: The force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
qa.e: From F = m × a, 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s². The weight of 1 kg on the Earth is about 9.8 N.

qa.q: When a moving bus brakes suddenly, the standing passengers tend to fall forward. Why?
qa.a: Their bodies tend to keep moving forward due to inertia
qa.e: The bus stops, but the passengers' bodies tend to continue in motion because of inertia, so they lurch forward.

qa.q: A coin is placed on a card over a glass. The card is flicked away quickly and the coin drops into the glass. This shows
qa.e: The card moves away so fast that the coin, at rest, tends to stay at rest and then falls into the glass.

qa.q: Which quantity is a measure of the inertia of an object?
qa.e: The greater the mass, the greater the inertia, and the harder it is to change the object's motion.

qa.q: A 50 kg girl runs at 4 m/s. What is her momentum in kg m/s?
Why does a fielder pull his hands backwards while catching a fast cricket ball?
qa.a: To increase the time of stopping the ball, so less force acts on his hands
qa.e: The ball's momentum must become zero. Spreading this change over a longer time needs a smaller force, so it hurts less.

qa.q: A gun recoils when a bullet is fired. Which law explains this?
qa.e: Total momentum before firing is zero, so after firing the forward momentum of the bullet equals the backward momentum of the gun.

qa.q: A 0.02 kg bullet leaves a 2 kg gun at 100 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the gun in m/s?
qa.e: Bullet momentum = 0.02 × 100 = 2 kg m/s. The gun gets 2 kg m/s backwards, so its speed = 2 ÷ 2 = 1 m/s.

qa.q: Which has the greatest inertia?
qa.e: The loaded truck has by far the greatest mass, so it has the greatest inertia.

qa.q: Who gave the universal law of gravitation?
qa.e: Isaac Newton stated the universal law of gravitation in the 17th century.

qa.q: If the distance between two objects is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
qa.e: Force is inversely proportional to d². Doubling d makes d² four times bigger, so the force becomes one-fourth.

qa.q: A boy has a mass of 60 kg on the Earth. What is his mass on the Moon?
qa.e: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change from place to place. Only weight changes.

qa.q: What is the weight, in newtons, of a 60 kg boy on the Earth? (Take g = 9.8 m/s².)
What is the approximate value of g near the Earth's surface, in m/s²?
qa.e: The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is about 9.8 m/s². About 1.6 m/s² is the Moon's value.

qa.q: In a tube with all the air removed, a feather and a coin are dropped together. What happens?
qa.e: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration g, whatever their mass.

qa.q: A stone weighs 60 N on the Earth. About how much will it weigh on the Moon, in newtons?
qa.e: The Moon's g is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so the weight becomes about 60 ÷ 6 = 10 N.

qa.q: What is the main cause of ocean tides on the Earth?
qa.a: The gravitational pull of the Moon
qa.e: The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth's oceans, making the water rise and fall twice a day at most places.

qa.q: A force of 20 N moves a box 5 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done, in joules?
A porter carries a suitcase on his head and walks along a level platform. How much work does he do against gravity on the suitcase?
qa.e: Gravity acts downwards but the suitcase moves horizontally, at right angles to the force, so no work is done against gravity.

qa.q: A motor does 1500 J of work in 10 s. What is its power in watts?
How many joules are there in 1 kWh?
A box slides across the floor and slows down. What kind of work does friction do on the box?
qa.e: Friction acts opposite to the direction of motion, so the work done by friction is negative.

qa.q: Asha pushes against a wall with all her strength, but the wall does not move. How much work has she done on the wall?
qa.e: Work needs displacement. The wall did not move, so no work is done on it.

qa.q: A 100 W bulb is switched on for 10 hours. How many units (kWh) of electricity does it use?
qa.e: Energy = power × time = 100 W × 10 h = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh = 1 unit.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of power?
qa.e: Power is measured in watts; 1 W = 1 J/s. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.

qa.q: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
qa.e: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

qa.q: A 10 kg box is lifted onto a shelf 5 m high. What is its gain in potential energy, in joules? (Take g = 10 m/s².)
If the speed of a scooter is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes
qa.e: KE depends on v². Doubling v makes v² four times bigger, so KE becomes four times as much.

qa.q: A stretched catapult (gulel) has which kind of energy?
qa.e: Energy is stored in the stretched rubber because of its changed shape. That is elastic potential energy.

qa.q: A mango falls from a tree. Ignoring air resistance, what happens to its energy as it falls?
qa.a: Potential energy turns into kinetic energy, and the total stays constant
qa.e: As height decreases, PE decreases and KE increases by the same amount, so the mechanical energy stays constant.

qa.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At its highest point, what is its kinetic energy?
qa.e: At the highest point the ball stops for an instant, so v = 0 and KE = 0. All its energy is potential energy then.

qa.q: Which statement is the law of conservation of energy?
qa.a: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another
qa.e: Energy only changes form. The total amount of energy in a closed system stays the same.

qa.q: A 2 kg coconut falls from a height of 5 m. What is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground, in joules? (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance.)
qa.e: All the starting PE (mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J) has changed into KE just before landing.

qa.q: A see-saw is which class of lever?
qa.e: The fulcrum (pivot) of a see-saw lies between the effort and the load, so it is a first-class lever.

qa.q: In a wheelbarrow, the load is between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort). Which class of lever is it?
qa.e: When the load is between the fulcrum and the effort, the lever is second class.

qa.q: Which of these is a third-class lever?
qa.e: In a fishing rod the effort (the front hand) is between the fulcrum (the hand at the end) and the load (the fish).

qa.q: A 200 N load is 0.5 m from the fulcrum. The effort arm is 2 m. What effort is needed, in newtons?
qa.e: Load × load arm = effort × effort arm, so 200 × 0.5 = effort × 2, giving effort = 50 N.

qa.q: A machine lifts a 300 N load when an effort of 100 N is applied. What is its mechanical advantage?
qa.e: MA = load ÷ effort = 300 ÷ 100 = 3.

qa.q: Why is a single fixed pulley used at a village well, even though it does not reduce the effort?
qa.a: It changes the direction of the effort, so you can pull down to lift up
qa.e: Pulling down is easier and safer because you can use your body weight. A fixed pulley has MA = 1 but changes the direction of force.

qa.q: What is the ideal mechanical advantage of a single movable pulley?
qa.e: Two parts of the rope share the load, so ideally the effort is half the load and MA = 2.

qa.q: Your forearm is a third-class lever with MA less than 1. What is its advantage?
qa.a: A small movement of the muscle makes the hand move a long way quickly
qa.e: Third-class levers need more effort than the load, but they give a gain in speed and distance of movement.

qa.q: Who discovered the electron?
qa.e: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays.

qa.q: Thomson's model of the atom is often compared to
qa.e: In Thomson's model, electrons sit in a positive sphere like seeds in the red part of a watermelon.

qa.q: In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
qa.a: Most of the atom is empty space
qa.e: If most particles meet nothing on their path, most of the space inside the atom must be empty.

qa.q: Very few alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil. What did Rutherford conclude from this?
qa.a: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
qa.e: Only a small, heavy, positively charged centre could push back a fast positive alpha particle, and it had to be tiny because so few hit it.

qa.q: Which particles did Rutherford fire at the gold foil?
qa.e: Rutherford used fast-moving, positively charged alpha particles.

qa.q: What was the main drawback of Rutherford's model?
qa.a: It could not explain why the atom is stable, since revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus
qa.e: A charged particle moving in a circle should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus. Real atoms are stable, so the model needed improvement.

qa.q: What new idea did Bohr add to the model of the atom?
qa.a: Electrons move only in certain fixed orbits without radiating energy
qa.e: Bohr proposed special orbits (shells) in which electrons do not lose energy. This explained why atoms are stable.

qa.q: Why did Rutherford choose gold for his foil?
qa.a: Gold can be beaten into extremely thin sheets
qa.e: Gold is very malleable, so a foil only about 1000 atoms thick could be made, letting alpha particles pass through.

qa.q: Who discovered the neutron?
qa.e: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

qa.q: The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of
qa.e: Atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus. It decides which element the atom is.

qa.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
qa.e: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.

qa.q: Chlorine-35 has atomic number 17. How many neutrons does it have?
qa.e: Neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18.

qa.q: What are isotopes?
qa.a: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers
qa.e: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.

qa.q: Which pair are isobars?
qa.e: Calcium-40 (Z = 20) and argon-40 (Z = 18) are different elements with the same mass number. The other pairs are isotopes.

qa.q: A neutral atom has 8 protons. How many electrons does it have?
qa.e: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the charges balance.

qa.q: What is the charge on a neutron?
qa.e: A neutron is neutral, as its name suggests. Protons are +1 and electrons are −1.

qa.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the L shell (n = 2) can hold?
qa.e: Maximum electrons = 2n² = 2 × 2² = 8.

qa.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the M shell (n = 3) can hold?
qa.e: Maximum electrons = 2n² = 2 × 3² = 18.

qa.q: What is the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11)?
qa.e: Fill K with 2, L with 8, and the last electron goes into M: 2, 8, 1.

qa.q: What is the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17)?
qa.e: K takes 2, L takes 8, and the remaining 7 go into M: 2, 8, 7.

qa.q: Magnesium has the configuration 2, 8, 2. What is its valency?
qa.e: Magnesium has 2 valence electrons, which it gives away to get an octet, so its valency is 2.

qa.q: Oxygen has the configuration 2, 6. What is its valency?
qa.e: Oxygen needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet, so valency = 8 − 6 = 2.

qa.q: Why does neon (2, 8) hardly react with other elements?
qa.a: Its outermost shell is complete with 8 electrons
qa.e: Neon already has a stable octet in its outer shell, so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

qa.q: Which element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 3?
qa.e: 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 electrons, so the atomic number is 13, which is aluminium.

qa.q: Which statement is the law of conservation of mass?
qa.a: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
qa.e: In a chemical reaction the atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass stays the same.

qa.q: 3 g of carbon combines completely with 8 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide is formed?
qa.e: By the law of conservation of mass, products = reactants = 3 + 8 = 11 g.

qa.q: Water from a well in Rajasthan and water from a lake in Kashmir are both purified. Which is true about them?
qa.a: Both have hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio, 1 : 8
qa.e: By the law of constant proportions, every sample of pure water has hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8.

qa.q: Which idea of Dalton's atomic theory was later shown to be wrong?
qa.e: Atoms are made of smaller particles (electrons, protons and neutrons), so they are not indivisible.

qa.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
qa.e: Sodium's symbol Na comes from its Latin name, natrium. S is sulphur.

qa.q: The symbol Fe stands for which element?
qa.e: Fe comes from 'ferrum', the Latin name for iron. Fluorine is F.

qa.q: What is the atomicity of ozone (O₃)?
qa.e: Atomicity is the number of atoms in one molecule. Ozone has 3 oxygen atoms.

qa.q: A negatively charged ion is called
qa.e: Anions carry negative charge, such as Cl⁻. Cations carry positive charge, such as Na⁺.

qa.q: One atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as
qa.a: one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom
qa.e: Scientists chose carbon-12 as the standard; 1 u is exactly 1/12 of its mass.

qa.q: What is the molecular mass of water, H₂O, in u? (H = 1, O = 16)
What is the molecular mass of carbon dioxide, CO₂, in u? (C = 12, O = 16)
What is the molecular mass of ammonia, NH₃, in u? (N = 14, H = 1)
What is the molecular mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, in u? (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
What is the formula unit mass of sodium chloride, NaCl, in u? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)
What is the formula unit mass of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, in u? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
Why do chemists use relative atomic masses instead of weighing single atoms in grams?
qa.a: Atoms are far too tiny to weigh one at a time, so they are compared with a standard atom
qa.e: A single atom's mass is extremely small, so it is easier to compare it with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom.

qa.q: Aluminium has valency 3 and oxygen has valency 2. What is the formula of aluminium oxide?
qa.e: Cross over the valencies: Al gets 2 and O gets 3, giving Al₂O₃.

qa.q: What is the formula of magnesium chloride? (Mg valency 2, Cl valency 1)
qa.e: Crossing over gives Mg₁Cl₂, written as MgCl₂.

qa.q: What is the formula of calcium hydroxide? (Ca valency 2, OH⁻ valency 1)
qa.e: Two hydroxide ions are needed, and the polyatomic ion goes in brackets: Ca(OH)₂.

qa.q: How many particles are there in one mole of a substance?
qa.e: One mole always contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant.

qa.q: How many moles are there in 36 g of water? (Molar mass of water = 18 g)
qa.e: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass = 36 ÷ 18 = 2.

qa.q: What is the mass of 0.5 mole of carbon dioxide (molar mass 44 g)?
qa.e: Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.5 × 44 = 22 g.

qa.q: What is the molar mass of oxygen gas, O₂? (O = 16 u)
qa.e: O₂ has two oxygen atoms: 2 × 16 = 32 u, so its molar mass is 32 g.

qa.q: Which contains more molecules: 1 mole of hydrogen gas (H₂) or 1 mole of carbon dioxide (CO₂)?
qa.e: One mole of any substance has 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Their masses differ, but the counts are the same.

qa.q: Sound of frequency 170 Hz travels at 340 m/s in air. What is its wavelength in metres?
What is the SI unit of frequency?
qa.e: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz); 1 Hz means one vibration per second.

qa.q: A girl's voice usually has a higher pitch than a man's. This means it has a
qa.e: Pitch depends on frequency. A shriller, higher-pitched voice has a higher frequency.

qa.q: When you strike a dholak harder, the sound becomes louder. What has increased?
qa.e: A harder strike makes the drum skin vibrate with a larger amplitude, which we hear as a louder sound.

qa.q: What is the normal range of hearing for humans?
qa.e: Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below are infrasound and sounds above are ultrasound.

qa.q: Two astronauts on the Moon cannot hear each other speak without radios, even standing close. Why?
qa.a: There is no air on the Moon, and sound needs a medium
qa.e: The Moon has almost no atmosphere. Sound needs a medium to travel, so it cannot pass through the vacuum between them.

qa.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its time period, in seconds?
In which medium does sound travel fastest?
qa.e: Particles in solids are tightly packed and strongly linked, so sound travels fastest in solids like steel. It cannot travel in a vacuum at all.

qa.q: A boy shouts near a cliff and hears the echo after 2 s. If sound travels at 340 m/s, how far away is the cliff?
qa.e: Sound travels 340 × 2 = 680 m in total, going to the cliff and back, so the cliff is 680 ÷ 2 = 340 m away.

qa.q: Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, what is the minimum distance from a wall needed to hear a distinct echo?
qa.e: The echo must take at least 0.1 s for the round trip: 340 × 0.1 = 34 m in total, so the wall must be 34 ÷ 2 = 17 m away.

qa.q: What does SONAR stand for?
qa.e: SONAR stands for Sound Navigation And Ranging. It uses ultrasound echoes to find distances under water.

qa.q: A ship's SONAR gets an echo from the sea bed after 4 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How deep is the sea?
How can reverberation be reduced in a school auditorium?
qa.a: By using curtains, carpets and sound-absorbing panels
qa.e: Soft, porous materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it, so repeated reflections die out quickly.

qa.q: How do bats find their way and catch insects in the dark?
qa.a: They send out ultrasound and listen for the echoes
qa.e: Bats send out high-pitched ultrasound squeaks, and the echoes tell them where obstacles and insects are. This is echolocation.

qa.q: What is a common medical use of ultrasound?
qa.e: Ultrasound scanners send ultrasound into the body and use the echoes to make images of organs, or of a baby in the womb.

qa.q: Why are the ceilings of many concert halls curved?
qa.a: To reflect sound evenly to all parts of the hall
qa.e: Curved ceilings and soundboards reflect sound so that it spreads evenly to the audience.

qa.q: Which part of the ear collects sound from the surroundings?
qa.e: The pinna is the outer, visible part of the ear. Its shape helps gather sound into the ear canal.

qa.q: The eardrum is also called the
qa.e: The eardrum is a thin, stretched membrane called the tympanic membrane. It vibrates when sound waves reach it.

qa.q: Which three tiny bones are in the middle ear?
qa.e: The hammer (malleus), anvil (incus) and stirrup (stapes) pass on and amplify the vibrations of the eardrum.

qa.q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
qa.e: The stirrup in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the human body.

qa.q: Which part of the ear changes vibrations into electrical signals?
qa.e: The fluid-filled cochlea in the inner ear has sensitive cells that change vibrations into electrical signals.

qa.q: Which nerve carries sound signals from the ear to the brain?
qa.e: The auditory nerve carries signals from the cochlea to the brain. The optic nerve is for the eye, the olfactory nerve for smell.

qa.q: What is the job of the Eustachian tube?
qa.a: To keep the air pressure equal on both sides of the eardrum
qa.e: It links the middle ear to the throat, so air can move in or out to balance the pressure, for example on a hill road or in a plane.

qa.q: Which is the best habit for protecting your hearing?
qa.a: Keeping earphone volume low and taking breaks
qa.e: Loud sound over a long time can damage the sensitive cells of the cochlea. Low volume and breaks protect them.

qa.q: How does Amoeba usually reproduce?
qa.e: A full-grown Amoeba divides its nucleus and then its cytoplasm to form two daughter cells.

qa.q: Which of these reproduces by budding?
qa.e: In yeast a small bud grows out from the parent cell and separates to live on its own.

qa.q: New Bryophyllum plants grow from
qa.a: buds on the margins of its leaves
qa.e: Bryophyllum (patharchatta) has buds along the notches of its leaf margins that grow into new plants.

qa.q: A filament of Spirogyra breaks into small pieces and each piece grows into a new filament. This is
qa.e: In fragmentation the body simply breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new individual.

qa.q: Bread mould (Rhizopus) spreads to new slices of bread by
qa.e: Rhizopus produces tiny spores in round sporangia. The spores travel through the air and grow on moist food.

qa.q: Which part of a potato grows into a new plant?
qa.e: A potato is an underground stem (tuber). Its 'eyes' are buds that sprout into new shoots.

qa.q: The malaria parasite Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells at the same time. This is called
qa.e: In multiple fission, one cell divides into many daughter cells at once.

qa.q: What is a disadvantage of asexual reproduction for a species?
qa.a: There is very little variation among offspring
qa.e: Asexual offspring are nearly identical, so if the environment changes, they may all be affected in the same way.

qa.q: What is the male reproductive part of a flower called?
qa.e: The stamen, made of an anther and a filament, is the male part. It produces pollen.

qa.q: Where are pollen grains produced?
qa.e: The anther, at the top of the stamen, makes pollen grains, which contain the male gametes.

qa.q: What is pollination?
qa.a: Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma
qa.e: Pollination only moves pollen to the stigma. Fertilisation, the fusion of gametes, happens later.

qa.q: Pollen from a flower on one mustard plant reaches the stigma of a flower on another mustard plant. This is
qa.e: Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen between flowers on different plants of the same kind.

qa.q: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into the
qa.e: The ovary swells and ripens into the fruit, which protects the seeds.

qa.q: After fertilisation, the ovule develops into the
qa.e: Each fertilised ovule becomes a seed containing the embryo.

qa.q: Inside the ovule, the zygote develops into the
qa.e: The zygote divides many times to form the embryo, which can later grow into a new plant.

qa.q: A flower is brightly coloured, sweet-smelling and full of nectar. How is it most likely pollinated?
qa.e: Colour, scent and nectar attract insects such as bees and butterflies, which carry pollen from flower to flower.

qa.q: What is the fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete called?
qa.e: Fertilisation is the fusion of the sperm and the egg to form a zygote.

qa.q: What is the single cell formed by fertilisation called?
qa.e: The zygote is the first cell of the new individual. It later divides to form the embryo.

qa.q: In frogs, where does fertilisation take place?
qa.e: Female frogs lay eggs in water and the male releases sperm over them, so fertilisation is external.

qa.q: A hen lays eggs, and fertilisation happens inside her body. Which describes a hen?
qa.e: In hens, fertilisation is internal, and the hen then lays eggs, so she is oviparous.

qa.q: Which of these animals is viviparous?
qa.e: A cow gives birth to a calf, so it is viviparous. Frogs, hens and crocodiles lay eggs.

qa.q: A tadpole is a stage in the life cycle of which animal?
qa.e: A frog's egg hatches into a tadpole, which changes into an adult frog through metamorphosis.

qa.q: In the life cycle of a silkworm, which stage lives inside the silk cocoon?
qa.e: The silkworm caterpillar (larva) spins a silk cocoon around itself and becomes a pupa inside it.

qa.q: What is a main advantage of sexual reproduction?
qa.e: Offspring get features from two parents, so they differ from each other. Variation helps a species survive when conditions change.

qa.q: Why do scientists classify living organisms?
qa.a: To make the huge variety of life easier to study and to show relationships
qa.e: Grouping organisms by similarities makes them easier to study and reveals how they are related.

qa.q: Which is the correct order of levels, from broadest to narrowest?
qa.a: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
qa.e: The hierarchy starts with the broadest group, Kingdom, and ends with the narrowest, Species.

qa.q: What is the basic unit of classification?
qa.e: The species is the smallest, most basic group: similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

qa.q: Which level contains the largest number of different kinds of organisms?
qa.e: Kingdom is the broadest level, so it includes the most kinds of organisms, which share only a few basic features.

qa.q: The tiger and the lion belong to the same genus, Panthera. What does this tell us?
qa.a: They are closely related and share many features
qa.e: Members of the same genus share many features and are closely related, but they are different species.

qa.q: Which basic feature separates bacteria from plants, animals and fungi?
qa.a: Bacteria are prokaryotic, with no nuclear membrane
qa.e: Bacteria have prokaryotic cells without a membrane-bound nucleus, while plants, animals and fungi are eukaryotic.

qa.q: A neem tree makes its own food, while a mushroom absorbs food from dead matter. Which feature of classification differs here?
qa.e: Making food (autotroph) versus taking food from outside (heterotroph) is a key feature used in classification.

qa.q: Which statement best defines a species?
qa.a: Similar organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring
qa.e: Members of a species can breed with each other to produce offspring that can themselves reproduce.

qa.q: Who introduced the system of binomial nomenclature?
qa.e: Carl Linnaeus gave every species a two-part scientific name in the 18th century.

qa.q: In the scientific name Mangifera indica, what does 'Mangifera' stand for?
qa.e: The first word of a binomial name is always the genus; the second is the species.

qa.q: In the scientific name of humans, Homo sapiens, which word must begin with a capital letter?
qa.e: The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter, so it is written Homo sapiens.

qa.q: What is the scientific name of the tiger, India's national animal?
qa.e: The tiger is Panthera tigris. Panthera leo is the lion, Felis catus is the house cat and Pavo cristatus is the Indian peafowl.

qa.q: Why do scientists use scientific names instead of local names?
qa.a: One scientific name is understood everywhere, while local names differ between places and languages
qa.e: A plant may have many local names, but only one scientific name, so scientists everywhere know exactly which species is meant.

qa.q: The lion is Panthera leo and the tiger is Panthera tigris. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: They belong to the same genus but are different species
qa.e: Both share the genus Panthera, but the different second words show they are different species.

qa.q: What is the scientific name of neem?
qa.e: Neem is Azadirachta indica. Mangifera indica is mango, Ficus benghalensis is banyan and Oryza sativa is rice.

qa.q: How should a scientific name be shown when it is handwritten?
qa.a: With the genus and species words underlined separately
qa.e: Handwriting cannot show italics, so each word of the name is underlined separately.

qa.q: Who proposed the five-kingdom classification?
qa.e: Robert Whittaker proposed the five kingdoms in 1969.

qa.q: To which kingdom do bacteria belong?
qa.e: Bacteria are prokaryotic and unicellular, which places them in Monera.

qa.q: Amoeba and Paramecium belong to which kingdom?
qa.e: They are single-celled eukaryotes, which places them in Protista.

qa.q: Mushrooms belong to the kingdom Fungi. Which feature do fungi have?
qa.e: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs with cell walls made of chitin.

qa.q: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) belong to which kingdom?
qa.e: Despite the name 'algae', cyanobacteria are prokaryotic bacteria, so they belong to Monera.

qa.q: Which kingdom has multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that depend on other organisms for food?
qa.e: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs whose cells have no cell wall.

qa.q: Which description fits the kingdom Plantae?
qa.a: They are multicellular autotrophs with cell walls
qa.e: Plants are multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls and chlorophyll for making their own food.

qa.q: How do most fungi get their food?
qa.a: By absorbing it from dead and decaying matter
qa.e: Most fungi are saprophytes: they release enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the digested food.

qa.q: Rocks, soil and mountains are part of which sphere?
qa.e: The lithosphere is the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.

qa.q: Which sphere includes all living organisms and the places where they live?
qa.e: The biosphere is the zone of life, where land, water and air meet and support living things.

qa.q: Which gas makes up most of the Earth's atmosphere?
qa.e: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air. Oxygen is about 21%.

qa.q: About what percentage of the air is oxygen?
qa.e: Oxygen is about 21% of the air. 78% is nitrogen, about 1% is argon and about 0.04% is carbon dioxide.

qa.q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
qa.e: About 71% of the surface is water, mostly oceans. Land covers about 29%.

qa.q: Where is the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun?
qa.e: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, above the troposphere where weather happens.

qa.q: What is the main source of energy for winds, the water cycle and photosynthesis on Earth?
qa.e: Sunlight heats the land, water and air unevenly, causing winds and evaporation, and powers photosynthesis.

qa.q: A volcano erupts: ash fills the air, lava covers fields and fish die in a nearby lake. What does this show?
qa.a: The Earth's spheres are connected, so a change in one affects others
qa.e: The eruption began in the lithosphere but changed the atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere too.

qa.q: What is the loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants called?
qa.e: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from plant leaves, mainly through stomata.

qa.q: Water vapour cools high in the sky and forms tiny droplets in clouds. What is this step called?
qa.e: Condensation is the change from water vapour (gas) to liquid droplets when it cools.

qa.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
qa.e: Green plants take in carbon dioxide to make food during photosynthesis. The other processes release carbon dioxide.

qa.q: Which of these adds carbon dioxide to the air?
qa.e: Burning fuels releases the carbon stored in them as carbon dioxide.

qa.q: In which plants do Rhizobium bacteria live in root nodules and fix nitrogen?
qa.a: Legumes such as gram and peas
qa.e: Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants and turns nitrogen gas into compounds that plants can use.

qa.q: Air is about 78% nitrogen. Why can't plants use this nitrogen directly?
qa.a: Plants can use nitrogen only after it is converted (fixed) into compounds such as nitrates
qa.e: Plants absorb nitrogen as compounds like nitrates from the soil. Bacteria and lightning fix nitrogen gas into such compounds.

qa.q: What do denitrifying bacteria do?
qa.a: Turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas
qa.e: Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas, completing the cycle.

qa.q: Which statement about matter and energy in the Earth system is correct?
qa.a: Matter is recycled, while energy from the Sun flows through in one direction
qa.e: Atoms of carbon, nitrogen and water are used again and again, but energy from the Sun passes through and leaves as heat.

qa.q: "It is raining heavily in Kolkata today." This statement describes
qa.e: It describes the atmosphere at one place for a short time, so it is about weather.

qa.q: "Rajasthan has hot, dry summers year after year." This statement describes
qa.e: It describes the usual weather pattern over many years, which is climate.

qa.q: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
qa.e: Carbon dioxide traps heat. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon, the main gases of air, do not act as greenhouse gases.

qa.q: What would happen if there were no natural greenhouse effect at all?
qa.a: The Earth would be much colder
qa.e: Greenhouse gases keep some of the Sun's heat near the surface. Without them, the Earth would be too cold for most life.

qa.q: What is the main human activity increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?
qa.a: Burning fossil fuels such as coal, petrol and diesel
qa.e: Fossil fuels release the carbon stored in them as carbon dioxide when they are burnt.

qa.q: Which is an effect of global warming?
qa.a: Melting glaciers and rising sea levels
qa.e: A warmer Earth melts ice on land, and the extra water plus warmer, expanding oceans raise sea levels.

qa.q: Why are hill stations like Shimla and Ooty cooler than the plains?
qa.a: They are at a higher altitude, and temperature falls with height
qa.e: Air temperature generally decreases with altitude, so places high in the mountains are cooler.

qa.q: Why does Mumbai have a milder climate than Delhi?
qa.a: Mumbai is closer to the sea, which moderates temperatures
qa.e: The sea heats and cools slowly, keeping coastal places from getting very hot or very cold.
